Kherson residents say they live in fear as the city is under constant drone threat from Russian forces.

The shaky video that has horrified viewers around the world lasts just over 30 seconds.

It shows an exploding drone — small enough to fit in the palm of the hand and loaded with explosives — circling just meters above a vegetable seller's market stall in an area near the southern Ukrainian city of Kherson.

The distinctive buzzing of the aircraft is audible throughout the short video. Costing maybe only a few hundred euros, one-way attack drones like this are controlled by pilots using onboard cameras that provide a first-person view.

The Ukrainian vendor immediately recognizes the danger. He takes cover behind a white van parked beside his stall, constantly looking up at the threat above.

Like a predator stalking its prey, the drone circles, chasing him around the vehicle before suddenly diving toward him. It explodes as it hits the ground beside the van.

Today, many were shocked by yet another video of the drone "safari" Russians are carrying out against civilians in Kherson. A Russian drone deliberately hunted down a man selling vegetables and detonated right next to him. The Russians even admitted to the crime, showing zero… pic.twitter.com/uGjC7esFwR

— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) August 4, 2026

The vendor miraculously survived the August 4 attack, though he suffered multiple shrapnel wounds to his arms, legs, and back, as well as a concussion.

The name of the man in the video is Yuriy. He is 52 years old and lives in neighboring Mykolaiv. He regularly travels to Kherson with his wife to sell vegetables.

"The drone came from somewhere behind the market, from those bushes over there, and it was flying very low," Yuriy said in a video interview from the hospital that was released by Ukrainian authorities. "It is an open area. There is nowhere to go. It is frightening. Really frightening,"

"The Russians have gone mad," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, describing attacks of this kind by Russian forces as deliberate strikes against civilians in Kherson.

What makes the attack on Yuriy unusual is not necessarily the attack itself, but the fact that it was captured in such detail on video.

WELT's reporting in Kherson since late 2024 — including from some of the worst-affected riverside districts such as Richport — has documented how Russian drone pilots regularly hunt people in the southern Ukrainian city, both soldiers and civilians alike.

Cars, ambulances, and pedestrians are targeted. Anyone can be hit at any time, residents say.

In Ukraine, these attacks have become known as Russia's "human safari."

"The Russians mostly attack cars and buses. There have also been many attacks on medical personnel and ambulances," Alexander Tolokonnikov, a spokesman for Kherson's military administration, told WELT.

Using his mobile phone, Tolokonnikov documents the different types of Russian attacks across the city. Since autumn 2024, explosive devices dropped or carried by drones have rained down with increasing frequency.

In recent months, Russian forces have dramatically intensified their drone attacks on civilians in the Kherson region. Residents have described the escalation, and official statistics provided by Tolokonnikov point to the same trend.

In January, four people were killed and 28 were wounded. In February, two were killed and 53 were wounded. March saw seven killed and 66 wounded; April, 12 killed and 147 wounded; May, 11 killed and 201 wounded; and June, 10 killed and 179 wounded.

Then came a dramatic surge in July: 26 people killed and 421 wounded by Russian drone attacks in a single month.

While WELT was unable to independently verify every individual case reported, the broader trend is unmistakable.

"This is clearly a war crime when they fly an explosive-laden drone directly into civilians or into an ambulance," Col. Markus Reisner, an Austrian military officer, told WELT.

Reisner has analyzed numerous videos of the drone attacks and believes there is a clear strategic calculation behind them.

"The Russians are trying in Kherson to drive the population away from the other side of the river and make this area uninhabitable," he said.

It is depopulation carried out with lethal precision.

The drone hunt against civilians has become part of Russia's approach to Kherson since Moscow lost control of the city.

In the first days after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin's troops seized central Kherson. The occupation lasted eight months.

During a Ukrainian counteroffensive, Russian forces were forced to retreat across the Dnipro River, and Ukraine liberated the city in November 2022.

Since then, Ukrainian and Russian forces have faced each other across the Dnipro, separated in places by only a few kilometers. The city is under fire day and night.

Over the past few years, WELT has confirmed multiple drone attacks on civilians in Kherson and spoken with the victims and local authorities.

Video footage of these hunts is sometimes openly displayed on pro-Russian Telegram channels.

The British non-profit Centre for Information Resilience (CIR) had already verified several such videos by the end of 2024. Its investigation found a "clear escalation" in drone attacks by Russian forces.

Olga Chernyshova survived one such attack in Kherson in September 2024.

A drone targeted her as she returned from shopping and parked her car.

"The drone was flying very low and making that noise. I immediately ran toward the house, and then it exploded behind me," Chernyshova said.

Her vehicle was badly damaged, but she escaped physically unharmed. In 2025, Chernyshova was running the last remaining shop in Richport, her heavily bombed neighborhood.

Volodymyr Shemenkov manages the last brewery on the outskirts of Kherson. Russian missiles have already struck its premises, as CCTV footage shows.

He said he personally knows numerous civilians who have been attacked by Russian exploding drones.

At the end of 2024, one of his workers was hit by a Russian drone attack as he stepped out of a taxi. "He was hit by a grenade dropped from a drone. It landed right next to his leg," Shemenkov told WELT last year.

His employee was taken to the hospital with serious injuries.

"If I tell you I'm not afraid, that would not be true. The truth is that every one of us is afraid. Nobody is safe anymore. When you walk down the street, you have to expect every second that a drone could hit you," Shemenkov said.

Before Russia's full-scale invasion, more than a quarter of a million people lived in Kherson. Most have fled; others are fighting at the front. Only around 50,000 to 60,000 residents remain.

Increasingly, everyday life is moving underground.

"Many of the people who are still here are fatalists," Aleksandra Kniga, who works with children and teenagers in Kherson, told WELT. "It is our fate whether we are killed in our homes or not. That is why we do not want to leave."

On April 2, Kniga experienced for herself just how omnipresent the threat of Russian drones has become.

She was walking through Kherson's Shumensky district looking for a new shelter for the children because the place they had previously been using had become too dangerous.

Previously, the neighborhood had been considered relatively safe.

"In April," Kniga said, "it became absolute hell." Drone attacks had increased dramatically.

As she walked through the streets, she said she heard shotgun fire getting closer and closer — apparent attempts to shoot a drone out of the sky.

Shortly afterward, her drone detector sounded an alarm. Devices like these are now carried by civilians as well as soldiers.

Kniga started running but could find almost no cover.

She just managed to reach the covered entrance of an apartment building when a drone came down nearby and exploded.

The blast left her with explosion-related trauma and a concussion. That the drone did not fragment into a large number of pieces probably saved her from more serious injuries, she said.

Every day, Kniga says, people in Kherson are wounded or killed by Russian exploding drones. Most attacks, however, are never captured on video.

At the same time, Russian propaganda repeatedly attempts to blame such attacks on Ukraine, or even claims that Ukrainians are killing their own civilians.

"This is the reality we live with," Kniga said. "This is how Russia terrorizes the people of Kherson every single day."

Ibrahim Naber is a foreign correspondent who has reported from Ukraine since 2022. In October 2025, he and his team were injured in a Russian Lancet drone strike in Dnipro. In 2025, he received the George Weidenfeld Prize for his coverage of global conflicts and crisis zones. He wrote his dissertation at King's College London on the psychology of modern drone warfare.

title: Moscow says it knows where Western ships sail as Putin threatens to seize vessels
description: The warning comes as European countries step up efforts to disrupt Russia's maritime oil trade and its so-called shadow fleet.
fullText:
Russian President Vladimir Putin threatens retaliation if Europe starts seizing Russian ships.

Russia's Pacific Fleet says it knows the routes and cargoes of Western commercial ships.

The warning comes as Europe ramps up pressure on Russia's shadow fleet, including naval boardings.

Moscow says it knows where Western commercial ships are sailing, as President Vladimir Putin threatens retaliation if Europe starts seizing Russian vessels.

The warning comes as European countries step up efforts to disrupt Russia's maritime oil trade and its so-called shadow fleet, part of a broader sanctions campaign aimed at squeezing Moscow over its war in Ukraine. In July, the European Union changed its sanctions rules to allow national authorities to sell Russian oil cargoes they have seized and confiscated.

On Wednesday, Putin described such seizures as "piracy and plunder," according to an official transcript from the Kremlin.

"If this happens, we will have to reciprocate — not necessarily in the waters where they plan to raid our own ships but anywhere we consider necessary or reasonable, including in the Pacific Fleet's area of responsibility," he said.

Pacific Fleet Commander Viktor Liina told Putin that Russia had conducted a "detailed analysis" of maritime traffic in the Asia-Pacific.

"We know the routes, what they are carrying, and whose ships they are," Liina said.

The threats come as European authorities step up action at sea.

In June, British forces boarded "Smyrtos," a sanctioned tanker the UK says belongs to Russia's shadow fleet. The vessel was subsequently held off England's south coast.

An EU naval mission has also boarded sanctioned tankers. On August 2, Italian forces operating under the EU's Operation Irini boarded "Toa Payoh," a sanctioned shadow-fleet tanker, in international waters to verify its nationality. It was the mission's second such operation in less than two weeks.

Oil and gas remain critical sources of revenue for Moscow, and Western governments have sought to squeeze those revenues through sanctions targeting Russia's energy trade and the ships used to transport its oil.

Russia's economy, meanwhile, is showing signs of strain. GDP grew 1.3% in the second quarter from a year earlier, according to Russia's Federal Statistics Service, reversing a 0.2% year-over-year decline in the first quarter.

Growth has slowed sharply from recent years, while borrowing costs remain high. The Bank of Russia's key interest rate stood at 14% in July.

Ukraine has also intensified attacks on Russia's energy infrastructure, striking refineries and other oil facilities in an effort to disrupt a major source of revenue for Moscow.

title: An overnight Ukrainian blitz damages Russia's Black Sea naval stronghold, Zelenskyy says
description: Ukrainian anti-ship missiles and drones blitzed a major Russian naval base on the Black Sea coast in a “unique” nighttime operation, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday.  Cutting-ed...
fullText:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian anti-ship missiles and drones blitzed a major Russian naval base on the Black Sea coast in a "unique" nighttime operation, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday.

Cutting-edge drones developed by Kyiv since Moscow's full-scale invasion over four years ago have repeatedly targeted Russian ships in the Black Sea, including warships and oil tankers.

Ukraine's air and sea drones have succeeded in limiting the movements of Russia's once-dominant Black Sea navy, Kyiv officials say, in one of the country's biggest accomplishments of the war.

But Ukrainian officials believe Russian President Vladimir Putin is bent on pressing ahead with the war, despite his bigger army's slow and costly progress on the battlefield and U.S. diplomatic efforts to find a settlement.

Putin is planning "an additional rapid mobilization of several hundred thousand Russians by the end of the year," Zelenskyy said Tuesday night on social media, citing Ukrainian intelligence reports.

Those reports have said recently that Russia is expanding production of ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, both of which are hard for Ukrainian air defenses to counter.

Ukraine also is trying to scale up its weapons manufacturing through agreements with partner countries.

Neither Putin nor other senior Russian officials have hinted at a possible major call-up of forces to fight in Ukraine. Some officials have accused Kyiv of trying to rattle the Russian public with talk of a mobilization.

Russian lawmaker Andrei Gurulyov brushed off reports of a possible autumn mobilization. "It is the enemy deliberately spreading rumors about mobilization in order to destabilize the situation inside Russia," he was quoted as saying by pro-Kremlin online outlet Tsargrad in comments published Monday.

After the widely unpopular partial mobilization of some 300,000 men four years ago, Russia has relied on volunteers attracted by relatively high pay. However, the decree declaring the partial mobilization that Putin signed in September 2022 is open-ended, allowing authorities to resume it if needed.

The Ukrainian military "carried out a unique operation targeting the naval base in Novorossiysk — the last major stronghold of the Russian fleet in the Black Sea," Zelenskyy said in a social media post Wednesday. The attack struck air defenses, piers and other port infrastructure, he added.

Russia relocated most of its naval ships to Novorossiysk after Ukrainian strikes on the main Black Sea base at Sevastopol on the Crimean Peninsula earlier in the war.

Hundreds of Ukrainian drones attacked Novorossiysk, Anapa and Gelendzhik and the Temryuk district of the Krasnodar region overnight, said Gov. Veniamin Kondratyev.

An 8-year-old child was one of three people killed in the attack on the region, Kondratyev said. He added that 24 others in the region were wounded. Dozens of residential buildings were damaged, Kondratyev said, and debris from downed drones fell on the grounds of four industrial plants.

The strikes damaged two of Novorossiysk's three grain terminals, with one of them halting operations, the Russian business daily Vedomosti reported.

Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed more than 500 Ukrainian drones.

Novorossiysk also is home to the Grushovaya oil terminal, one of the largest international hubs in southern Russia for petroleum products. No reports indicated it had been hit.

In February, the U.S. State Department expressed its displeasure about Ukraine's attacks on Novorossiysk, saying they affected U.S. oil interests in ⁠Kazakhstan.

The Caspian Pipeline Consortium operates a pipeline from the Caspian coast in northwestern Kazakhstan to Novorossiysk. The pipeline handles much of the crude exports from three major Kazakh fields in which major U.S. energy companies, Chevron and ExxonMobil, have stakes.

With the militaries of European countries boarding and detaining sanctioned Russian oil tankers at sea, hurting the country's trade and heaping economic pressure on Moscow, Putin on Wednesday threatened retaliation for what he termed "piracy."

Speaking on a visit to a Russian warship taking part in a naval exercise in the Pacific, Putin said Western countries are breaking international maritime law by seizing ships they say are part of Moscow's " shadow fleet " of sanctions-dodging merchant vessels.

"It's nothing but piracy and robbery," Putin said. "If this is done, we will be forced to respond in kind."

On the Crimean Peninsula, which was illegally annexed by Moscow in 2014, air defenses downed 115 Ukrainian drones over Sevastopol overnight, said Mikhail Razvozhayev, the city's Russian-installed head. He added that 10 apartment buildings and 25 private houses were damaged.

Ukraine's air force said Russia fired 138 long-range drones as well as an unspecified number of missiles during the night, with damage recorded at 16 locations.

In the Kherson region of southern Ukraine, a large-scale Russian drone attack overnight killed two people and wounded two others, said regional head Oleksandr Prokudin.

The attacks also destroyed a shopping mall in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, according to authorities.

Missiles and long-range drones hit fuel reservoirs and infrastructure used for unloading and storing military cargo in the port of Chornomorsk in Ukraine's Odesa region, Russia's Defense Ministry said.

A bulk cargo vessel carrying military equipment and a tanker loaded with oil for the Ukrainian armed forces also were hit in Odesa, it said.

Follow the AP's coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Russia is helping China close gap with US forces amid Taiwan tensions, warns longtime military leader
description: Retired Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery warns Russia is giving China submarine quieting technology that could erode a key U.S. Navy undersea advantage.
fullText:
Sound alarms are blaring over an escalating partnership between Russia and China to subvert the U.S. military amid rising hostility between the world powers.

Retired Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery tells Fox News Digital that Moscow may be providing Beijing with technology to make its submarines harder for the U.S. Navy to detect, potentially eroding a key military advantage in the tensions over Taiwan.

"Russia is giving incredibly important technology to China. They're allegedly giving them submarine quieting technology," Montgomery, co-author of the new book "Axis of Aggressors," told Fox News Digital.

Three Key Reasons Why America Cannot Afford To Lose Taiwan To Communist China

Montgomery said Russian forces are providing the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) with submarine-quieting technology, an area where China has long sought to improve its capabilities. Such a transfer, he warned, could weaken a critical U.S. advantage in undersea warfare — a gap that has long favored American forces.

"Any weakening of our asymmetric advantage in undersea warfare is a big deal," he cautioned.

The Navy says its submarine force relies on technological superiority and stealth to maintain its undersea advantage, while China has continued to face weaknesses in submarine propulsion and quieting even as it rapidly modernizes its fleet.

Quieting technology reduces a submarine's acoustic signature, making it harder to detect and track. Russian assistance in that area could help Beijing narrow the gap, complicating the U.S. Navy's ability to find Chinese submarines in a potential future conflict over Taiwan's independence from the CCP.

The Chinese Embassy did not directly address whether Beijing has received Russian submarine-quieting technology when reached by Fox News Digital.

"Military cooperation between China and Russia consistently adheres to the principles of non-alliance, non-confrontation, and non-targeting of third parties, playing a significant role in safeguarding the sovereignty and security of both nations and maintaining international and regional peace and stability," the embassy said in a statement. "We hope that relevant parties will view China-Russia military cooperation objectively and rationally, and stop groundless speculation."

The embassy said Taiwan is China's internal affair and urged the U.S. to safeguard stability in the bilateral relationship and across the Taiwan Strait.

Montgomery's warning echoes concerns raised by Adm. Samuel Paparo, commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, who told the Senate Armed Services Committee in April 2025 that China was receiving "potentially submarine quieting help" from Russia.

Us Falls Behind In Hypersonic Race As China, Russia Gain Edge

Paparo said China's backing of Russia's war effort — including machine tools and legacy chips — was part of a broader exchange in which Moscow was returning assistance in military areas where it holds particular strengths.

The exchange reflects a deepening relationship in which Russia and China are increasingly providing capabilities the other lacks, Montgomery said.

"This transactional relationship is putting the United States and its most important allies and partners at risk," he said.

Paparo sounded a similar warning in November 2024, saying he expected Russia to provide China submarine technology that could help close America's undersea advantage. He described the relationship between Moscow and Beijing as a "transactional symbiosis."

China, meanwhile, has helped Russia rebuild its defense industrial base during the war in Ukraine. Paparo told senators Beijing provided 70% of the machine tools and 90% of the legacy chips that enabled Moscow to rebuild its war machine.

Montgomery said China's support extends beyond those supplies.

"And then China has backstopped the whole thing," Montgomery said, pointing to increased Chinese foreign direct investment and trade with Russia as well as components used in Moscow's ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles.

The support has helped keep Russia's economy and war machine operating, Montgomery argued.

In return, he said, Moscow is increasingly providing Beijing with military technology it had previously been reluctant to share — including the alleged submarine-quieting assistance.

In October 2024, the Treasury Department said a Russian defense firm coordinated production of Garpiya attack drones at factories in China, using Chinese-made engines and components before the weapons were transferred to Russia for use in Ukraine.

Russia has provided Beijing with more direct military assistance as well. A 2025 RUSI investigation, based on leaked Russian contracts and correspondence, found that Moscow agreed to equip and train a Chinese airborne battalion and transfer technology that could help Beijing develop similar capabilities itself.

Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine is now in its fifth year, with no ceasefire agreement in place despite continued diplomatic efforts. The prolonged war has deepened Moscow's dependence on Chinese industrial and financial support while giving Russia battlefield experience and military technologies that could be valuable to Beijing in a future Taiwan contingency.

For the U.S., the stakes are particularly acute around Taiwan. American submarines are central to U.S. planning for a potential Indo-Pacific conflict, and quieter Chinese vessels could make it harder to track, deter and counter the People's Liberation Army Navy in waters surrounding the island.

Montgomery said the possible transfer reflects the broader argument of "Axis of Aggressors," America's adversaries are increasingly trading the capabilities each lacks, creating challenges that span Europe and the Indo-Pacific.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Russian embassy for comment. U.S. Indo-Pacific Command declined to comment.

title: Ukraine pounds grain terminals at Russia's Black Sea Novorossiysk port
description: Ukraine hammered Russia's Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk in a massive overnight drone attack that put two major grain terminals out of action, according to Russian industry
fullText:
Aug 12 (Reuters) - Ukraine hammered Russia's Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk in a massive overnight drone attack that put two major grain terminals out of action, according to Russian industry sources, raising fears in global markets of a disruption to supplies.

Russia is the ‌world's largest wheat exporter and most of those exports are shipped via its Black Sea ports like Novorossiysk. Russia's main grain lobby group ‌warned last month that Ukrainian attacks could shut down grain exports via the Black Sea in the near future, pushing up prices and causing hunger in Africa and the Middle East.

Ukrainian ​President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Telegram that Ukraine had hit Russia's Novorossiysk naval base with drones, missiles and unmanned boats. Russia moved some of its Black Sea Fleet vessels to Novorossiysk after Kyiv's forces attacked them repeatedly in Crimea, which Moscow seized and annexed from Ukraine in 2014.

Veniamin Kondratyev, the governor of Krasnodar region, where Novorossiysk is located, said a "massive" wave of Ukrainian attacks had targeted the area and killed at least two people, including an 8-year-old child.

Andrei Kravchenko, ‌the mayor of Novorossiysk, said the Black Sea port's ⁠water supply had been suspended and an emergency situation had been declared following the attack, which damaged four unspecified enterprises, more than two dozen residential buildings and some educational facilities.

Unverified video on social media showed images of a tower ⁠of flames and smoke rising from somewhere in Novorossiysk.

Amid fears of disruptions to wheat supplies on global markets, Chicago wheat futures rose around 3% on Wednesday following reports of the Novorossiysk attack.

Russian strikes on ships in the Black Sea have drastically reduced grain shipments from Ukraine, which is also a major grain exporter. Shipments tumbled ​76% ​in the first two weeks of August, versus the same period last year, Ukraine's ​agriculture ministry said.

REPORT OF DEAL ON OIL SHIPMENTS

Novorossiysk also hosts ‌oil export infrastructure, including for the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), which is owned partly by U.S. oil majors Chevron and Exxon Mobil and carries Kazakh oil exports to market.

The Financial Times reported on Wednesday that, following a request from U.S. Vice President JD Vance in late July, Ukraine had agreed not to target CPC infrastructure and non-Russian vessels, as long as they were not under Ukrainian sanctions or carrying Russian oil or other cargo.

Ukraine's presidency did not respond to a request for comment on the story.

There was no indication that the CPC or tankers collecting oil from the pipeline had been struck ‌during the overnight attacks.

In Sevastopol in Crimea, more than three dozen drones were downed, ​the city's Russian-installed governor, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said on Telegram.

Separately, a Russian attack caused a fire ​at a shopping mall in the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, ​regional Governor Ivan Fedorov said on Telegram, posting pictures of a building ablaze.

A Russian attack on Odesa, Ukraine's largest ‌seaport, damaged infrastructure there, Serhiy Lysak, head of the city's ​military administration, said on Telegram, without giving ​details.

Moscow has intensified its strikes on Ukraine's logistics and warehouse facilities in response to Kyiv's attacks on Russian energy, port and logistic hubs.

Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Kyiv had handed proposals to U.S. negotiators for a plan to end the conflict, which started when Russia launched ​its full-scale war on Ukraine in February 2022.

Ukraine has ‌repeatedly called for a ceasefire after nearly 4-1/2 years of fighting. Russia says it wants a settlement, but any solution must ​involve Ukraine fully ceding four regions Moscow claims as well as resolving the conflict's "root causes."

title: Putin says Russia will start seizing European vessels if its ships targeted
description: President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday that Russia will respond in kind if European countries start to seize Russian merchant vessels
fullText:
MOSCOW, Aug 12 (Reuters) - President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday that Russia will respond in kind if European countries start to seize Russian merchant vessels and the commander of Russia's ‌Pacific Fleet said his forces were ready to "inspect and detain" foreign vessels from what he called hostile states.

The comments, ‌which Putin made as he oversaw navy drills in Russia's far east, come as the EU tries to ratchet up pressure on Russia's so-called shadow fleet, ​expanding sanctions against hundreds of vessels and detaining some ships and their crews for checks. Some European governments have said they are exploring tougher maritime enforcement measures against ships suspected of sanctions evasion.

"We can see that the authorities of certain countries, in violation of international maritime law, are attempting to restrict the movement of our economic operators' vessels..., and have recently gone so far as to ‌consider the possibility of seizing our vessels and ⁠selling off the property they have plundered from us," Putin said.

"Naturally, this is nothing less than piracy and robbery. And if this begins to be put into practice, we shall be forced to ⁠respond in kind. And not necessarily in those waters where raids on our ships and vessels are planned, but wherever we ourselves deem it necessary and appropriate."

Viktor Liina, commander of Russia's Pacific Fleet, told Putin that what he described as hostile countries such as Britain ​and France ​also transported goods on vessels flying flags of convenience which - if ​the EU and Britain's own language was used - could ‌also be described as a "shadow fleet."

"Western states are actively using vessels flying the flags of third countries to transport cargo in their own interests. In essence, this constitutes their shadow fleet," Liina told Putin.

"We have the capabilities to inspect and detain vessels belonging to unfriendly states and their shadow fleet; inter-agency coordination is in place, and we are ready to tackle these tasks."

He said his fleet had carried out a detailed analysis of maritime traffic in the Asia-Pacific region and knew the routes, the cargo, ‌and ownership of vessels linked to unfriendly nations.

The Russian Foreign Ministry weighed ​in too, accusing the EU in a statement of using its naval ​force in the Mediterranean - named operation EUNAVFOR MED Irini ​and originally launched to enforce a U.N. arms embargo on Libya - of carrying out unlawful inspections of ‌foreign vessels.

It cited a search operation led by ​Italy which boarded a tanker from ​Russia's so-called "shadow fleet" this month, the second such operation in less than two weeks as Europe intensifies scrutiny of vessels suspected of helping Moscow circumvent oil sanctions.

"Operation Irini is effectively being used by the European Union to intimidate commercial ​shipping companies and impede freedom of navigation. ‌There is a clear abuse of existing international legal norms and an expansive interpretation of its powers," the ​foreign ministry said.

"By resorting to such actions, the European Union is...bringing great dangers upon itself."

title: Zelenskiy: Ukraine has given US negotiators proposals for ending the war with Russia
description: Aug 11 () - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukraine had handed proposals to U. negotiators for a plan to end the war with Moscow and suggested that Russia ‌would use its parliamenta...
fullText:
Aug 11 (Reuters) - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukraine had handed proposals to U.S. negotiators for a plan to end the war with Moscow and suggested that Russia ‌would use its parliamentary election next month as a pretext to declare a new mobilisation.

Zelenskiy's announcement ‌of fresh proposals for peace talks, largely stalled since the outbreak of the conflict with Iran, comes amid suggestions by both ​Russia and Ukraine that U.S. negotiators would soon pay a visit to their two countries.

"We have conveyed our proposals to the American side," Zelenskiy said in his nightly video address.

"And the United States can help strengthen our defence, first and foremost with air defence, and put pressure on Russia so that its plans are different -- to ‌prepare for an end to the war ⁠rather than prolonging it."

Zelenskiy offered no details on the proposals.

U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were last in Moscow last January and have not yet visited Kyiv.

Ukraine ⁠has repeatedly called for a ceasefire after nearly 4-1/2 years of fighting. Russia says it wants a settlement, but any solution must involve Ukraine fully ceding four regions Moscow claims as well as resolving the conflict's "root causes."

In his ​remarks, ​Zelenskiy said Ukrainian intelligence had evidence that Russia would exploit ​its September "pseudo-election" -- a reference to restrictions imposed ‌on the polls -- to proclaim a new mobilisation to boost the numbers of fighting personnel.

"They are preparing for mobilisation in the autumn, immediately after the imitation of parliamentary elections," Zelenskiy said as part of a plan to "create the appearance that Russians supposedly support the war."

"Then, following the so-called election, he plans an additional rapid mobilisation of several hundred thousand Russians by the end of the year, plus another similar number next year."

The ‌draft, he said, would be in addition to recruitment through ​the conclusion of contracts with servicemen.

The Putin-backed United Russia Party ​and other broadly pro-Kremlin parties are set to ​retain their dominance in the Russian parliament after the vote.

Russia's Supreme Court on Monday ‌barred the liberal Yabloko party, the only officially ​registered party that opposes ​Moscow's war in Ukraine, from competing in the election.

Russia declared a "partial mobilisation" in 2022 after the launch in February of its full-scale invasion. Zelenskiy has previously suggested that Moscow would introduce a new ​mobilisation.

Russian officials have declined to discuss ‌the issue.

Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, one of Russia's most ardent hawks, said last month ​that Russia needed no new mobilisation as 200,000 volunteers had signed contracts in the first ​half of 2026.

title: Ukraine halts strikes on tankers using Russian port at US request, FT says
description: Ukraine has paused drone strikes on oil tankers using Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiysk after a request from U.S.
fullText:
Aug 12 (Reuters) - Ukraine has paused drone strikes on oil tankers using Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiysk after ‌a request from U.S. Vice President JD Vance, the Financial ‌Times said on Wednesday, citing Ukrainian officials.

The paper said last month's request followed ​U.S. alarm that Ukraine was destabilising oil markets and harming U.S. firms by targeting tankers carrying crude piped from Kazakhstan to a Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) terminal at the port.

Ukraine agreed not to target CPC infrastructure ‌or non-Russian vessels as ⁠long as the latter were not under Ukrainian sanctions and were not carrying Russian oil or cargo, ⁠the newspaper added.

The White House, State Department and Vance's office did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment outside business hours. Reuters ​could not ​immediately verify the report.

Ukrainian forces recently ​stepped up strikes on Russian ‌energy infrastructure and other sites in an effort Kyiv says aims at depriving Russia of resources to fund its military.

Black Sea drone attacks took out as much as a fifth of CPC oil loadings in July, four sources familiar with the data said, as the ‌Russia-Ukraine war spilled over to hit ​sales by Kazakhstan and western oil majors.

Kazakhstan, ​which relies on the ​CPC route for crude exports, suffered a drop of ‌14% in oil production in ​July versus June, ​the sources said. Chevron and Exxon Mobil are among the major Western oil companies operating there.

A U.S. official confirmed to the ​paper that the ‌administration had warned Ukraine to stop attacking non-Russian vessels in ​the Black Sea.

title: Russian attacks kill 10 in Ukraine as Zelenskyy says Moscow is getting more North Korean missiles
description: Russia attacked Ukrainian cities with missiles, drones and glide bombs Tuesday, killing at least 10 civilians, officials said, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Moscow is getting new military help...
fullText:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia attacked Ukrainian cities with missiles, drones and glide bombs Tuesday, killing at least 10 civilians, officials said, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Moscow is getting new military help from North Korea for its more than 4-year-old invasion.

Zelenskyy said Russian forces used ballistic missiles supplied by North Korea in an overnight attack on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia, where a company said seven workers at its steel plant were killed and 21 injured.

Three more people, including a 15-year-old boy, were killed by Russian drones and artillery in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, authorities said.

In addition to the ballistic missiles, North Korea is preparing to deploy more of its troops to Russia, Zelenskyy said late Monday.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un signed a strategic partnership agreement in 2024, pledging mutual aid if either country faces aggression.

Kim has sent thousands of troops and huge supplies of weapons to support Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Some experts say the engagement with Moscow is helping improve North Korea's military capabilities, and Zelenskyy said the battlefield experience would help Pyongyang menace other countries in its region.

Ukraine says Russia is scaling up its production of ballistic missiles, aiming to exploit Kyiv's critical shortage of Patriot air defense interceptors that can stop them, and claims Moscow is preparing to recruit more troops for a new push on the front line that stretches 1,250 kilometers (775 miles) along eastern and southern Ukraine.

"Every step Russia takes — increasing ballistic missile production, bringing in North Korean equipment, preparing for mobilization — all of this shows that Moscow is preparing not for peace, but for escalation," Zelenskyy said on social media.

In an unusual step, Ukraine's air force didn't say in its daily report how many missiles Russia launched overnight. It was not clear whether the omission was deliberate, and Kyiv officials made no immediate comment.

U.S.-led diplomatic efforts to stop the war have fizzled as Washington grew frustrated with the lack of progress and its attention turned to the Iran war.

In an indication that Putin is determined to press on with the invasion, Russia's highest court on Monday ordered that Yabloko, the only political party opposing the war, to be excluded from the ballot in the Sept. 18-20 parliamentary election.

"The Kremlin will not enter serious negotiations or make meaningful compromises on its demands as long as Putin believes that he has a viable military path to achieving his full objectives," the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said in an analysis Monday.

"Ukraine's Patriot shortages offer Russia an opportunity to cause very serious damage to Ukraine over the coming winter and will therefore contribute to delaying meaningful negotiations and protracting the war," it said.

Russian forces also struck parts of the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, overnight, according to officials. One strike hit the grounds of a children's hospital, leaving two craters and shattering windows, the State Emergency Service said. Children and medical workers were in bomb shelters and nobody was hurt, it added.

At another location in Kyiv, a Russian strike started a fire in a warehouse that spread across about 1,200 square meters (nearly 13,000 square feet), according to emergency officials.

The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces overnight struck "military industrial facilities and transport and logistics centers" in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia with "ground-based precision weapons."

It said in a statement that it hit civilian storage facilities housing drones in Kyiv and a metallurgical plant in Zaporizhzhia.

Metinvest, a major Ukrainian mining and metals company with operations in Zaporizhzhia, said seven of its steel plant employees died as staff tried to reach shelters after a warning of an incoming ballistic missile.

The company, which employs tens of thousands of people, said in a statement that the attack damaged its blast furnace and other equipment and forced the plant to shut down.

Russia targeted Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia with Zircon anti-ship missiles and Iskander ballistic missiles, while launching 120 long-range strike drones across the country, Ukraine's air force said.

Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said its air defenses overnight intercepted nearly 400 Ukrainian drones over 14 regions and Crimea, the peninsula that Moscow illegally annexed from Kyiv in 2014.

Russia's biggest online retailer, Wildberries, said its logistical facilities in the Voronezh region near the Ukrainian border came under attack and caught fire. It added that the fire was extinguished and goods stored there were "largely undamaged."

Ukraine has repeatedly struck Wildberries warehouses and Russian oil facilities in what it says is a strategy to compel Putin to negotiate an end to the invasion.

Ukraine's General Staff said its forces struck an oil refinery in the city of Orsk in Russia's Orenburg region near the border with Kazakhstan, about 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukraine, causing a fire.

The refinery, with an annual processing capacity of about 44 million barrels of crude oil, produces gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel, among other products. The extent of the damage was being assessed, the military said.

Meanwhile, Romania's Ministry of National Defense said its navy destroyed two drones drifting in the Black Sea about 90 nautical miles (166 kilometers) from the port of Constanta.

The Gerbera-type drones were neutralized by divers using controlled detonations, and some pieces were recovered, the ministry said, adding that Ukraine said the drones were not theirs.

The United Nations, meanwhile, estimates that more than 16,000 civilians detained by Russia during the war are still being "deprived of their liberty," with many held incommunicado and on grounds that don't comply with international law.

"Widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment" of both Ukrainian civilian detainees and prisoners of war by Russia are continuing, including sexual violence, said Claudia Fuentes Julio, the U.N. assistant secretary-general for human rights.

She spoke at an informal meeting of the U.N. Security Council on Monday to spotlight the plight of civilians and soldiers taken following the Russia invasion.

Edith M. Lederer at the United Nations contributed.

title: Russia frees ailing ex-US Marine Robert Gilman from detention
description: Russia on Tuesday freed a former American Marine who had been jailed in the country since 2022, U. In a social media post, Trump said Russia agreed to release Robert Gil...
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Russia on Tuesday freed a former American Marine who had been jailed in the country since 2022, U.S. President Donald Trump said.

In a social media post, Trump said Russia agreed to release Robert Gilman, 32, for humanitarian ‌reasons after discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin, adding that the ailing American would arrive at Joint Base Andrews near Washington on Tuesday night.

"I am ‌proud to announce that American Citizen Robert Gilman, a former United States Marine, is coming HOME!" Trump said. "We appreciate this decision, and the fact that Russia asked for no one in return — No exchange ​took place."

The White House and the State Department had urged Moscow to release Gilman so he could receive medical treatment in the United States. U.S. officials said Putin approved a pardon for him.

Gilman was being held in a prison in Voronezh, about 340 miles (550 kilometers) south of Moscow. The exact circumstances of his health are unclear.

But Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer of Global Reach, an advocacy group representing Gilman's family, told Reuters last week that Gilman was moved in late June from the prison hospital to the psychiatric ward ‌of a civilian emergency hospital in a catatonic-like state assessed ⁠as a "dissociative stupor."

A U.S. official who spoke to Gilman said he was walking and talking.

"All things considered he seems to be in good shape," the official said.

Trump's post included a photo of a gaunt-looking man on a plane surrounded by a group of ⁠smiling people carrying an American flag. The president said he had spoken to Gilman, who requested a cheeseburger upon landing.

"I will take care of that!" Trump said.

Gilman will be evaluated on the flight by four doctors, said the U.S. officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

After that, Gilman is likely to be flown to a rehabilitation center in San Antonio, Texas, for ​medical ​treatment, the officials said.

ARRESTED OVER POLICE OFFICER INCIDENT

Gilman, who served in the U.S. Marines from August ​2019 until August 2020, was traveling by train when he was ‌arrested in January 2022 in Voronezh, Lebson said.

He was detained for allegedly kicking a police officer while drunk, according to Russian state media.

However, his father, Vladimir Gilman, who emigrated to Massachusetts from Russia, wrote in an October 2024 Boston Globe op-ed that the charges were false.

His son, he said, had fallen ill when the incident occurred and accidentally kicked the officer. The officer was uninjured, dropped the charges, and did not present evidence at Gilman's trial, he wrote.

Robert Gilman was sentenced to 4-1/2 years in jail. He was one of at least 10 Americans known to be imprisoned in Russia.

The U.S. officials said a Russian senior official, Yuri Ushakov, informed Trump aides ‌last week that Putin had agreed to sign a decree pardoning Gilman for humanitarian purposes, given ​Putin's friendship with the president.

The release resulted from intense negotiations over the weekend by U.S. and ​Russian officials. The U.S. did not exchange any Russian prisoners in order to ​gain Gilman's release and no concessions were made, the officials said.

"It's a goodwill gesture," one official said.

Trump thanked U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, ‌senior director for counterterrorism Sebastian Gorka, his son-in-law Jared Kushner, ​and U.S. special envoy for hostage response Adam ​Boehler for making the release possible.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Gilman is among 100 U.S. citizens whose freedom Trump has helped secure during his second term in office. Rubio said the U.S. appreciated the "positive step," but called for the release of other Americans who he said were unjustly ​detained in Russia, including Stephen Hubbard.

Hubbard, a retired schoolteacher, was ‌sentenced in October 2024 to almost seven years in a penal colony after a court found him guilty of serving in a Ukrainian territorial ​defense unit against Russian forces, tasked with manning a checkpoint.

title: Russia rolling out Starlink-style network faster than expected, Kyiv says
description: KYIV, Aug 10 () - Russia is rolling out its own version of the Starlink satellite internet system faster than expected and plans ‌to have nearly 300 satellites in orbit by 2027, according to ‌a Ukrain...
fullText:
KYIV, Aug 10 (Reuters) - Russia is rolling out its own version of the Starlink satellite internet system faster than expected and plans ‌to have nearly 300 satellites in orbit by 2027, according to ‌a Ukrainian intelligence official.

SpaceX's Starlink network, which operates in Ukraine but not Russia, has given Kyiv ​a major advantage in drone operations and battlefield communications.

Russian forces had been using grey-market Starlink terminals in Ukraine until Kyiv successfully lobbied SpaceX to disable them earlier this year, one of several factors that shifted battlefield momentum in Ukraine's ‌favour.

In an interview with Ukrainian ⁠media outlet RBC-Ukraine, Major General Vadym Skibitskyi said Russia currently has 16 satellites in its Rassvet system.

"They have already begun ⁠launching it much faster than originally planned," said Skibitskyi, who is the deputy head of Ukraine's GUR military intelligence service.

The system can currently operate only intermittently ​when one ​of the satellites passes over Ukrainian territory, ​he said. However, Russia plans ‌to create a constellation of 292 satellites by 2027 and 924 by 2035, he added.

"Once Russia deploys a full satellite constellation, the system will operate like Starlink. Discussions are already underway on how to counter it," he said.

Russia has been pounding Ukraine with an array of supersonic missiles as ‌Kyiv has depleted its stock of interceptor ​missiles.

Skibitskyi said Moscow had already met its annual ​production targets for Zircon and ​Oniks missiles in the first seven months of the year ‌and was exceeding its 2026 missile ​production goals by ​10% to 20%.

He said Ukraine's emerging ballistic missile industry, along with drone production facilities, had become a priority target for Russia's missile campaign.

Skibitskyi added ​that Russia's stockpile of ‌Iskander-M ballistic missiles, the mainstay of its supersonic strikes, was estimated ​at around 130, with 65 new ones made in July.

title: Taiwan's war drills showcased a new strike drone class that Ukraine used to smash Russia this year
description: Taiwan's navy deployed two fixed-wing propeller drones, which officials described as "mid-size suicide drones" that were locally built.
fullText:
Taiwan showcased two midsize strike drones above its southwest coast on Saturday.

Their designs and descriptions draw easy comparisons to Ukraine's mid-range drones.

Such drones likely give Taiwan the ability to cheaply hit a Chinese invasion force over the horizon.

TSOYING, TAIWAN — Taiwan's navy deployed two medium-class strike drones on Saturday for the island's biggest annual military exercise, and their designs resemble those of the loitering munitions giving Ukraine fresh wins against Russia this year.

The pair of fixed-wing, propeller-driven drones appeared during a littoral combat drill simulating an attack on Tsoying, Taiwan's southwest coast.

It was the first time these drones were shown at the Han Kuang exercise, Taiwan's annual rehearsals against a Chinese invasion.

As the drones loitered for about 30 minutes above the beach, Taiwanese military officials described them to reporters as "medium-size suicide drones," adding they were locally built. The island's National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology designs and manufactures the vast majority of Taiwan's homegrown weapons.

"The drone used was provided by the Armament Bureau to the navy for testing purpose," a spokesperson for Taiwan's navy told Business Insider.

They declined to comment on the drone's specifications or whether its design was influenced in any way by the recent wars in Ukraine or the Middle East.

The one-way drones were not shown attempting to launch an attack, and it's unclear whether they represent Taiwan's final designs for the aircraft.

Ukraine has been using similar fixed-wing drones to attack Russian forces roughly 30 to 300 km behind the front lines this year, mainly disrupting supply routes that the Kremlin has relied on to funnel resources to the war.

Tsoying, where Taiwan hosts its largest naval base, is about 295 km, or 183 miles, from mainland China.

"The desire to employ more medium-range drones fits into things that Taiwan has learned from Ukraine," said Bryce Barros, a visiting fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, a Taipei think-tank backed by the Taiwanese government.

Mid-range drones would fill a gap in Taiwan's littoral defense with a cheaper way to strike Chinese forces or weapons from "over-the-horizon" as they approach the island, Barros said.

Unlike Ukraine's plains and forests, Taiwan's littoral defense covers a strait notorious for bad winds and volatile sea states, suggesting that Taipei may want its own drone built to withstand poor weather.

Instead of air defense systems or supply trucks like in Ukraine or Crimea, Taiwan's mid-range drones would likely target slow-moving vessels transporting troops or weapons, Barros added.

"A range of 40 kilometers to 60 kilometers would be very useful for a whole host of different platforms, anything to make it more difficult for the PLA to start getting into Taiwan's territorial waters," he said, referring to the People's Liberation Army.

Taiwan's government has said that it plans to produce 100,000 drones a month by 2030. In June, its national defense ministry proposed a $6.6 billion budget to procure over 210,000 domestically produced attack, reconnaissance, and sea drones.

It's all part of the island's emerging "hellscape" strategy, which aims to hamper Chinese forces attempting to cross the Taiwan Strait by flooding it with thousands of aerial, surface, and underwater drones.

The littoral drills on Saturday, attended by Taiwanese president Lai Ching-te, also featured naval special forces deploying in the island's homegrown M109 Skyship rigid-hull inflatable boats.

Taiwan's navy and coast guard launched rapid sorties with four of its older, 170-ton Kuang Hua-6 missile boats and at least one Anping-class patrol vessel — a newer, 750-ton catamaran that can be fitted with anti-ship missiles during wartime.

The Han Kuang exercise, which lasts 10 days and 9 nights this year, features island-wide drills to simulate how Taiwanese forces and civilian institutions would respond to Chinese gray-zone tactics and an invasion.

August 10, 2026: This story was updated to reflect the romanized spelling of Tsoying.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Moscow, Kyiv assassins hunt weapons bosses as Ukraine war spills beyond the battlefield
description: Draganfly CEO Cameron Chell says drone company leaders are now primary targets as Russia and Ukraine race for battlefield AI and autonomy advantages.
fullText:
A dangerous new front is emerging in the Russia-Ukraine war as attackers and alleged intelligence operatives increasingly target executives and engineers developing the cutting-edge drone technology that is reshaping the battlefield, industry experts warned Sunday.

The attacks include an Aug. 4 car bombing near Yekaterinburg that critically injured Vladimir Tkachuk, head of Russian drone manufacturer Uraldronzavod, and killed his driver, according to Russian state news agency TASS, The Associated Press reported.

His company produces the "Upyr," or "Ghoul," a first-person-view attack drone used by Russian forces in Ukraine.

'A New Kind Of War': Inside Ukraine's Hidden Factories Mass-producing Combat Drones

Days earlier, Andrei Cherezov, head of another Russian drone company, was shot three times in Tula overnight July 28-29 in an apparent assassination attempt, according to Ukrainian outlet Pravda. Authorities have not publicly attributed either attack to Ukraine.

Draganfly CEO Cameron Chell told Fox News Digital that the rise in attacks comes as Russia and Ukraine race for an edge in drone warfare, making the relatively small number of people responsible for developing new technology increasingly important targets.

"When you can't take out all the distributed infrastructure, drone manufacturing leadership becomes the primary target," Chell said.

"These strikes in Russia and Ukraine and Germany on founders, leaders, engineers of defense and, in particular, drone-type companies are down to drones and these companies having such an impact themselves."

Ukraine's Battlefield Is Transforming The Future Of Nato

"Because drone technology evolves rapidly — often with significant iterations occurring every 10 to 30 days — targeting a key engineer, founder, or product lead creates immediate operational disruptions on the battlefield."

"Taking out a particular engineer or taking out a particular leader can set a very important weapons program back quite some time and disrupt shipments to the front line," Chell added.

German authorities have also arrested two suspected operatives accused of spying on a Bavarian drone manufacturer for Russian intelligence, while reports this month said the alleged operation included preparations to target company executive Stefan Thumann, according to Germany's Die Zeit.

The case follows a reported 2024 plot disrupted by U.S. and German intelligence to target Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger.

Zelenskyy Announces 'The Future Is Here' After War's First All-robot Capture

Chell said as Ukraine and Russia push toward artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons systems, engineers developing those technologies are more strategically important.

"What we see in the Ukraine-Russia conflict is nobody in the loop — total autonomy is the direction things are going because it moves with more speed and precision," Chell said.

"AI and total autonomy are the big innovations for the next 18 months, so a potential reason we could see more targeted activity against leaders is because Ukrainians have that technology advantage."

"Targeting small drone companies is a relatively easy operation compared to targeting individuals in state-run weapons programs," he said.

"It is a fairly inexpensive, low-risk tactic for intelligence agencies that yields an immediate impact on the battlefield, and that's why we've seen this tactic."

"It is a very interesting turn or tactic that's being played by both sides here."

Chell highlighted how Russia and Ukraine approach such plots differently.

"I wouldn't suggest one side has an advantage over the other in terms of tactics, but psychologically, it has a deeper effect on the Russian side," Chell said.

Ukraine Unleashes More Than 400 Drones Near Moscow In One Of War's Biggest Attacks

"The volume of drone advantage will remain with the Russians for the foreseeable future, but the innovation of drones, tactics, and technology lies with the Ukrainians right now."

"Ukraine faces an existential threat, so they are ready for anything. Their tactics tend to be much more blunt — a direct shooter in a hallway or a car bomb," he added.

"The Russian tactics tend to be much more state-organized, using old Cold War tactics: low-level contacts, extensive intelligence and surveillance ahead of time, and inserting into other countries like Germany," he said.

"The Russians have a long-standing, well-established intelligence infrastructure dating back to World War II and the Cold War."

Trump Is Proving That The Way To Better Our Military Is To Secure Our Supply Chains

As the drone manufacturing industry takes greater precautions, Chell maintained that threats against companies and individuals in the defense supply chain are receiving increased scrutiny.

"We are very cognizant of it, and we're in contact with the proper authorities to make sure we're taking precautions on both a cyber and physical level to ensure we're at less risk," he said.

"We certainly don't take anything for granted."

"There are training and programs in place to ensure executives have a level of safety, primarily around awareness, cybersecurity, and physical location protection," Chell added before stating that the attacks and attempted assassinations have "heightened the conversation around it."

"We as an industry are taking it with a measured amount more seriously," he said.

title: Syria will take back control from Russia of 2 key Mediterranean bases under a new deal
description: Russian forces in Syria will give up control of two strategic bases on the Mediterranean coast, which will be used as joint Russia-Syrian training centers under a new agreement between the two countri...
fullText:
DAMASCUS, Syria (AP) — Russian forces in Syria will give up control of two strategic bases on the Mediterranean coast, which will be used as joint Russia-Syrian training centers under a new agreement between the two countries, Syria's Foreign Ministry said Sunday.

Russia was the top political and military ally of ousted President Bashar Assad during the country's civil war between 2011 and 2024. Assad was ousted in December 2024 by Islamist insurgents led by current interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa and has since fled into exile in Russia.

Throughout the conflict, the Hmeimem air base and the Tartus naval base were key Russian military outposts in the eastern Mediterranean.

Under the new agreement between Damascus and Moscow, Syria will take control of the Hmeimem air base and the commercial berth at Tartus port as part of its civil administration. The military facilities at both sites will become "joint training" centers, the Foreign Ministry said.

The new arrangements represent a "reorganizing of the Russian presence" along Syria's coast, the ministry said.

"This move marks the most significant development since negotiations began approximately a year and a half ago, paving the way for a new phase in Syrian-Russian relations," the statement read.

Russia did not immediately comment on the agreement.

Moscow did not interfere during the lightning insurgency that led to Assad's overthrow, but it provided the longtime Syrian leader and his family asylum. After Assad's ouster Russian troops remaining in Syria gradually left the country except for those stationed at the bases.

Syria's new leadership has aimed to maintain strong bilateral ties with Moscow. Al-Sharaa has visited President Vladimir Putin in Moscow twice since taking power, with the two Mediterranean bases being key points of discussion.

Since Assad's ouster, Syria has also bolstered its ties with the United States, Europe, and neighboring Arab countries that had cut ties with Damascus during Assad's crackdown on protests. Washington has lifted most of its crippling sanctions on the country, and French President Emmanuel Macron made a visit to Syria in July during which he announced that the two countries would appoint respective ambassadors for the first time in 14 years.

title: A Russian retail giant’s warehouse burns after Ukraine's latest long-range drone attack
description: Ukrainian long-range drones hit a warehouse of Russia’s biggest online retailer in the Ural Mountains, more than 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) from the two countries’ border, local officials and the ...
fullText:
Ukrainian long-range drones hit a warehouse of Russia's biggest online retailer in the Ural Mountains, more than 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) from the two countries' border, local officials and the company said Friday.

Ukraine has regularly hit targets in the distant Urals this year and has even struck a Russian oil refinery in western Siberia, nearly 2,500 kilometers (1,550 miles) from the border. The attacks are examples of how Kyiv has used drone innovation as a key part of its response to the invasion by its much bigger enemy more than four years ago.

Its successes have drawn international interest and drone cooperation agreements with nine countries, with further deals being negotiated with 15 other countries, according to Kyiv officials.

Wildberries said its warehouse in Yekaterinburg, Russia's fourth-largest city, was set ablaze by the attack. Most merchandise wasn't damaged, the company said, unlike at some of the more than a dozen other Wildberries depots struck by Ukraine in recent weeks that have burned down.

The regional governor, Denis Pasler, said three drones hit the warehouse's roof. Artyom Zhoga, the Kremlin's representative in the region, said that 800 people were evacuated from the warehouse and nobody was hurt.

Kyiv is trying to rattle the Russian public and the Kremlin with the attacks.

Russian President Vladimir Putin chaired a meeting Friday of the country's Security Council. He said in televised opening remarks that the meeting would focus on additional measures to "strengthen … protection of infrastructure facilities" but gave no further details.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is pushing for his country to keep up the pace of technological development, especially in air defense systems to help stop Russian ballistic missiles that are exploiting Ukraine's shortage of American-made Patriot interceptor missiles and battering civilian areas.

A joint European anti-ballistic development program is already underway, Zelenskyy said late Thursday, with 10 countries engaged in developing an anti-ballistic shield. Europe is concerned about Moscow's ambitions on the continent beyond Ukraine.

"Ukraine is capable of producing its (anti-ballistic) missile and launcher, while our partners will provide the necessary components and critical elements — radars, sensors, and everything else required," Zelenskyy said on social media. "An anti-ballistic program of our own — one that is truly large-scale — will greatly benefit everyone in Europe."

At the same time, Ukraine is working on manufacturing its own ballistic missiles to use against Russia. "The tests have shown strong potential. We need to turn this into a real weapon," Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian front-line defenses in eastern regions, meanwhile, remain under strain as Russia's bigger army looks for a breakthrough after months of minimal advances that Western analysts and officials say have had a high cost for Moscow in troop casualties.

Ukraine has been evacuating children from Kramatorsk, one of the four eastern Donetsk region cities that make up the Ukrainian so-called Fortress Belt. The line of four large and heavily defended cities, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) long, has been key to denying Moscow its goal of seizing Ukraine's industrial heartland.

The head of the Donetsk region's regional military administration, Vadym Filashkin, said Friday that more than 800 people, including 91 children, were evacuated over the previous 24 hours.

Ukraine has been deploying midrange strike drones to disrupt Russia's supply lines and slow its advance.

Zelenskyy said that the recently appointed commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian armed forces, Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi, reported to him Friday about the military situation in Donetsk.

He said in a social media post that they reached "an understanding of how to strengthen" Ukraine's defenses there but gave no details.

Russia's air defenses downed 203 Ukrainian drones from late Thursday through early Friday, the Defense Ministry in Moscow said.

Over the past week, the Russian military struck 31 bulk cargo vessels and three tugboats that operated "in the interests of the Ukrainian armed forces," it said.

It added that late Thursday two ships were hit by Geran-4 drones in the Black Sea east and southeast of Odesa and one was struck in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk.

In other attacks, the ministry said that the military hit a facility assembling long-range drones in Okhtyrka in the Sumy region on Thursday. It also released a video of a train purportedly carrying military equipment struck by a Geran drone and then an Iskander ballistic missile near Vyshneve in the Dnipropetrovsk region.

Meanwhile, Russia attacked Ukraine with 147 long-range strike drones overnight, according to the Ukrainian air force.

In Ukraine's northern Sumy region, a Russian drone struck a busy market Friday morning, wounding 10 people, authorities said.

Russia also launched glide bombs and drones of various types at the regional capital, according to the head of regional administration, Oleh Hryhorov.

The attack targeted residential buildings, transport and infrastructure, wounding two people, he said.

title: Crowded Russian beach descends into chaos after alleged Ukrainian drone incident kills 7, including 4 children
description: A projectile struck a crowded Russian Black Sea beach Monday, killing seven people, including four children, and injuring 58. Russia blamed a Ukrainian drone attack as video captured the deadly impact...
fullText:
Vacationers were sent scrambling for safety Monday after a projectile struck a crowded beach in a Russian Black Sea resort town, killing seven people, including four children, and injuring dozens more, officials said.

Video footage captured the incident in the village of Arkhipo-Osipovka near Gelendzhik, where the beach was packed with visitors at the time of the strike.

The Russian Mission in Geneva said in a post on X that the "bloody attack" was carried out by a drone launched by Ukraine, accusing Kyiv of targeting civilians.

Ukraine Launches What Appears To Be One Of Its Largest Drone Attacks Against Russia: Report

"The attack targeted civilian infrastructure. Emergency and special services are working at the crash site," regional Gov. Veniamin Kondratyev said in a post on Telegram.

"What happened today is a targeted attack by the Kyiv regime against civilians who have no connection to the military infrastructure. This cynical and inhumane terrorist attack against children cannot be justified."

Ukraine Unleashes More Than 400 Drones Near Moscow In One Of War's Biggest Attacks

Andriy Kovalenko, an officer with Ukraine's Defense Forces, disputed Russia's account, saying the deaths were directly caused by Russian air defenses that intercepted a drone, sending debris onto the beach.

Zelenskyy Says Putin 'Lost The Initiative' As Ukraine's Tech Industry Reshapes The War

title: Ukrainian attacks on Wildberries strike at heart of Russia Inc
Opinion - This winter, Putin will feed even more of Russia’s youth into the meat grinder
description: Russian President Vladimir Putin is a cornered man. Ukraine, especially through its deep-strike drones and ballistic missiles, is bringing Putin’s special military operation home to the city confines ...
fullText:
Russian President Vladimir Putin is a cornered man. Ukraine, especially through its deep-strike drones and ballistic missiles, is bringing Putin's special military operation home to the city confines of Moscow and Saint Petersburg.

As of this writing, 15 distribution hubs of Wildberries — Russia's equivalent of Amazon, which is frequently used to supply troops with equipment the Russian state fails to supply — have been hit or destroyed by Ukraine. Likewise, most of Putin's largest oil refineries, including one as far away as Siberia, have been struck.

Billowy black smoke from burning Wildberries and uncertainty at the gas pump are putting domestic pressure on the Kremlin in ways never felt since the war began in February 2022.

Putin must either go big or go home. Going home probably means the end of his regime, so going big in Ukraine is really his only option. All signs indicate that he intends to do so this winter, whatever the cost.

Putin is not going to use nuclear weapons, although he can be counted on to threaten and bluff with them. No — going big for him means doubling, if not tripling down on his meat grinder approach to the war in Ukraine. Mass infantry attacks are his military strategy. If a Russian operation fails on the frontlines, his typical response is simply to try it again with larger numbers. This is why, in the first half of 2026, Russia has suffered roughly eight casualties the for every one it has inflicted on Ukraine.

The paradox of Putin's stratagem is that, during the first four years of the war, as he has ramped up his investment of Russian lives in the conflict, he has gotten diminishing returns. Russian casualties, dead and wounded, are fast-approaching 1.5 million, with little accomplished on the battlefield.

The Institute for the Study of War estimates that as of late July, Russia had gained only 81 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory this calendar year. In fact, since January 2023, the Kremlin has seized only about 5 to 6 square kilometers while incurring 925 casualties each day on average since 2023.

Undeterred, Putin will keep squeezing harder/ With the repeated failures of his spring and summer ground offensives, he will weaponize the coming winter once again, calculating that he will enjoy a new strategic opening in the compounding Patriot interceptor shortage in Ukraine and Europe's indecision over establishing a No-Fly Zone.

In July, Moscow increased its widescale aerial attacks on Ukraine. According to Militarnyi, Russia fired "107 ballistic missiles and 20 3M22 Zircon [hypersonic] missiles," which was a significant surge from June. Likewise, according to Ukrainian Colonel Oleksandr Zaruba, Russian drone attacks have substantially increased as well "to wage a war of attrition against Ukraine's air defenses."

Although Russia is firing off missiles faster than it can produce them, it has apparently struck a new deal with North Korea to augment its ballistic missile stockpile. "A North Korean missile unit has begun deploying to western Russia and could be equipped with 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers for strikes against Ukraine," Reuters reports.

So Putin is again betting on destroying Ukraine's critical infrastructure, including its electrical power grid, to bring the country to its knees during the coldest months of the coming year. This follows the same old playbook: Hit the grid, pressure the population, then launch another spring offensive to seize all of the Donbas. This is supposed to force Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and his generals to capitulate.

But here's the problem: Another large-scale Russian military operation will require a new mobilization of conscripts and reserves. Russian casualties in Ukraine so far in 2026 continue to exceed recruitment of new soldiers.

Putin is unlikely to issue new mobilization orders until after the Russian Duma elections in September. That means the new Russian conscripts or reserve call-ups used in 2027 will be hastily trained and poorly equipped. They will be no match for Ukraine's established kill zones or the country's battle-hardened armed forces on the frontlines.

Putin is desperate for a win in the Donbas. Will he get it? Almost certainly not. But he will bleed hundreds of thousands of Russian soldiers in the process of finding out.

Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. They are the cofounders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

title: Terrifying 'human safaris' on display in shocking video that reveals depths of Russia's deadly campaign

fullText:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of going "mad" following the release of a video showing a Ukrainian vegetable vendor being stalked by a Russian military drone before the drone exploded near him.

The incident occurred on Aug. 4 at a Kherson market located in Southern Ukraine. Footage released by the Kherson Regional Military Administration shows a drone hovering near a man standing beside a minibus before following him as he moves behind the bus. Moments later the drone dives toward the minibus and explodes near its front, detonating close to where the man is standing.

"A Russian drone deliberately hunted down a man selling vegetables and detonated right next to him," Zelenskyy wrote on X in a post including the video. "The Russians even admitted to the crime, showing zero regret and openly boasting about tormenting people. The man was wounded in the blast. Every single day, ordinary people in Kherson face these Russian "safaris."

Moscow Bombing Exposes Potential Security Gaps Around Putin's Military Elite, Expert Says

The street vendor, identified as 52-year-old Yuriy, survived the near-fatal encounter, which Ukrainian authorities describe as part of a pattern of Russian drone attacks that track and target civilians — a practice they have dubbed "human safaris."

Speaking from a hospital bed, Yuriy told BBC that he and his wife were setting up their stall when he heard the drone buzzing nearby. His wife had run away, and the drone zeroed in on Yuriy, who pulled out vegetables to show that he did not have a weapon.

"It could see that I had tomatoes out, some cucumbers and eggplants laid out on the floor," Yuriy told BBC. "It even ducked under the umbrella when I was running away round the other side."

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the attack a "barbaric war crime," demanding international intervention.

Why Trump Is Downplaying Reports Russia And China Are Helping Iran

Zelenskyy argued that everyone should see the video to make clear what Russia is capable of, arguing that President Vladimir Putin won't stop with Ukraine.

"This is not just about Ukraine," Zelenskyy wrote. "Russia's campaign against human life must be stopped here in Ukraine before it spreads further. Finland and Kazakhstan, the Baltic states and Poland, the countries of the South Caucasus, Romania, and Moldova — all should work together to ensure real security guarantees and bring Russia's war to an end."

"Peace is needed, which requires cooperation among everyone in the world who truly values peace," Zelenskyy wrote.

Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office says authorities have opened 5,303 criminal cases into drone attacks on civilian targets in the Kherson region. The office says the attacks have killed 287 civilians and wounded 2,549 others, including 41 children.

Ukraine Seeks More U.s. Patriot Interceptors As Bomb Shelter Probe Deepens

Prosecutors said the attacks appeared to be part of a systematic campaign, with FPV drones repeatedly striking civilians in public places, homes, transport hubs and civilian vehicles, and in some cases launching follow-up attacks after emergency crews arrived.

The release of the chilling video comes a year after a one-year-old boy was killed by a Russian drone in the Kherson region while playing in his playpen in his grandmother's backyard.
